content: Ethanol, also known as ethyl alcohol, is a flammable, colorless, and slightly toxic chemical compound. It is most commonly recognized as the active ingredient in alcoholic beverages. Its molecular formula is represented as EtOH, CH3CH2OH, C2H5OH, or its empirical formula C2H6O, which it shares with dimethyl ether. The fermentation of sugar into ethanol is one of the earliest organic reactions known to humanity, and its intoxicating effects have been recognized since ancient times. In modern times, ethanol is also produced industrially from byproducts of petroleum refining. Due to its ease of production and relatively low toxicity, ethanol is widely used as a solvent in products intended for human contact or consumption, such as perfumes, flavorings, colorings, and medicines. In chemistry, it serves as both an essential solvent and a fundamental feedstock for synthesizing other products. Ethanol burns cleanly and has a long history as a fuel, including its use in internal combustion engines. Ethanol has been utilized by humans since prehistoric times as the intoxicating component of alcoholic beverages. Archaeological evidence, such as dried residues on 9,000-year-old pottery from northern China, suggests its use even among Neolithic peoples. The isolation of ethanol as a relatively pure compound was first achieved by Persian alchemists during the Abbasid Caliphate, with notable contributions from Al-Razi. The writings attributed to Jabir Ibn Hayyan (Geber) mention the flammable vapors of boiled wine, and Al-Kindi described the distillation of wine. Absolute ethanol was first obtained in 1796 by Johann Tobias Lowitz through charcoal filtration. Antoine Lavoisier identified ethanol as a compound of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, and in 1808, Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure determined its chemical formula. Fifty years later, Archibald Scott Couper published a structural formula for ethanol, making it one of the first chemical compounds to have its structure determined. Michael Faraday prepared ethanol in 1828 via acid-catalyzed hydration of ethylene, a process similar to modern industrial ethanol synthesis. Ethanol was used as lamp fuel in the United States as early as 1840, but taxes during the Civil War rendered its use uneconomical until the tax was repealed in 1906. By 1908, ethanol was used to power early Model T automobiles. However, during Prohibition in 1920, ethanol fuel fell out of favor due to its association with moonshiners. Recent increases in oil prices have renewed interest in ethanol as a fuel. The physical properties of ethanol are largely influenced by its hydroxyl group and the shortness of its carbon chain. The hydroxyl group allows ethanol to participate in hydrogen bonding, making it more viscous and less volatile than less polar organic compounds of similar molecular weight. Ethanol is flammable, colorless, and has a strong odor. It is a versatile solvent, miscible in all proportions with water and many organic solvents, including acetic acid, acetone, benzene, and diethyl ether. Ethanol's miscibility with water contrasts with longer-chain alcohols, whose water solubility decreases as the carbon chain length increases. Hydrogen bonding causes pure ethanol to be hygroscopic, readily absorbing water from the air. The polar nature of the hydroxyl group enables ethanol to dissolve many ionic compounds, such as sodium and potassium hydroxides, magnesium chloride, and ammonium salts. Ethanol also dissolves nonpolar substances, including essential oils and various flavoring, coloring, and medicinal agents. Mixtures of ethanol and water exhibit unusual phenomena, such as a reduction in volume compared to their individual components. Ethanol-water mixtures with greater than 50% ethanol are flammable and easily ignited. Solutions with less than 50% ethanol may also be flammable if vaporized by heating, as in certain cooking methods. Ethanol is classified as a primary alcohol, meaning the carbon atom to which its hydroxyl group is attached has at least two hydrogen atoms. Its chemistry is largely determined by the hydroxyl group. The hydroxyl proton is weakly acidic, even weaker than water. Ethanol can be converted to its conjugate base, the ethoxide ion, by reaction with alkali metals like sodium. Under specific conditions, ethanol reacts with hydrogen halides to produce ethyl halides, such as ethyl chloride and ethyl bromide. Ethyl halides can also be synthesized using specialized halogenating agents like thionyl chloride or phosphorus tribromide. Acid-catalyzed reactions of ethanol with carboxylic acids produce ethyl esters and water, provided water is removed from the reaction mixture. Ethanol can also form esters with inorganic acids, such as diethyl sulfate and triethyl phosphate, which are useful ethylating agents in organic synthesis. Ethanol can be oxidized to acetaldehyde and further to acetic acid, with these reactions catalyzed by enzymes in the human body or by strong oxidizing agents in the laboratory. Combustion of ethanol produces carbon dioxide and water. Ethanol is produced both as a petrochemical, through the hydration of ethylene, and biologically, by fermenting sugars with yeast. The economic viability of each process depends on the prevailing prices of petroleum and grain feedstocks. Industrial ethanol is often synthesized via acid-catalyzed hydration of ethylene, using phosphoric acid as a catalyst. Ethanol for alcoholic beverages and fuel is primarily produced by fermentation. Yeast, particularly Saccharomyces cerevisiae, metabolizes sugar in the absence of oxygen to produce ethanol and carbon dioxide. The fermentation process must exclude oxygen to prevent yeast from undergoing aerobic respiration, which produces carbon dioxide and water instead of ethanol. Starchy materials, such as cereal grains, must first be converted into sugars for fermentation. This is traditionally achieved by malting, which produces the enzyme amylase to convert starches into sugars. For fuel ethanol, starch hydrolysis can be accelerated using dilute sulfuric acid or fungal amylase. Cellulosic ethanol is derived from cellulose, a component of plant cell walls. The high cost of cellulase enzymes has historically limited its production. However, advancements in enzyme technology and genetic engineering have made cellulosic ethanol more feasible. Cellulose-containing agricultural byproducts, such as corn cobs and straw, can be converted into fermentable sugars. Hemicellulose, another polysaccharide in plant material, decomposes into five-carbon sugars like xylose, which are not metabolized by Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Other microorganisms are being investigated for their ability to ferment xylose into ethanol. Ethanol is widely used as a motor fuel and fuel additive. Brazil has a robust ethanol industry, producing ethanol from sugarcane, which has a higher sucrose concentration and is easier to process than corn. The United States primarily produces ethanol from maize. Ethanol is commonly blended with gasoline, with a 10% ethanol blend known as gasohol. Ethanol's role as a fuel oxygenate has increased following the phase-out of methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE) due to groundwater contamination concerns. Ethanol is also used as an antiseptic, killing microorganisms by denaturing proteins and dissolving lipids. It is effective against most bacteria, fungi, and many viruses but is ineffective against bacterial spores. Additionally, ethanol serves as an antidote for poisoning by methanol or ethylene glycol, competing for the alcohol dehydrogenase enzyme and preventing the formation of toxic metabolites. Ethanol's versatility extends to its use as a solvent in perfumes, paints, and tinctures, as well as in design markers. It is a central nervous system depressant with significant psychoactive effects, making it the principal active ingredient in alcoholic beverages. Ethanol's metabolism in the human body involves oxidation to acetaldehyde and acetic acid, processes catalyzed by enzymes.
